utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning, technicians; good morning to our interpreters, our legal clerks; good morning, counsel for the Prosecution, counsel for the Defence; good morning, General Krstic. We will resume our hearing in the Krstic case. The appearances are the same, for the record. And if I could have the witness brought into the courtroom, please. I believe it's still Witness N.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. He's a protected witness, and we'll have to draw the blinds. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours; good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the public, let me just say that the blinds will be pulled down while the witness is being brought in, and after that they will be pulled up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness N. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had a restful night? Did you sleep well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just remind you that you are still under an oath and that you will continue answering questions that will be put to you by Mr. Harmon. Thank you. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness N.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When we concluded your testimony yesterday, you were describing your journey from a warehouse in Bratunac to a school somewhere in the area of Zvornik, and you had left the warehouse sometime on the 13th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, approximately what time did you arrive at the school that was located in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was past midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you arrived in the early morning, then, of the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Had you ever been to that school before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, would you tell the Judges what happened once you arrived at the school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once we arrived in the schoolyard, the buses stopped and the Serb soldiers approached the buses. The buses opened -- the doors of the buses opened and people started coming out in columns. They were going in the direction of a gym, of a gymnasium, and they were getting into that gym. At that moment, the doors of my bus opened as well and we got out, and we passed by some Serb soldiers and went in the direction of the gym, and we entered the gym and sat down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you got off the bus, Witness N, approximately how many Bosnian Serb soldiers did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 15 and 20, 15 to 20 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do you recall how those soldiers were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour of the camouflage? Was it a police camouflage uniform or was it an army camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: An army camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said you went into a gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- 19/5 placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, I'm going to show you a photograph, an interior photograph of a gymnasium, and I'm going to ask you if you can identify this particular photograph. The usher will place it on the ELMO and you'll be able to see it on the monitor in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's not very visible on the monitor. Perhaps, Mr. Usher, if you could show this photograph to the witness first and then we can place it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, is this the gymnasium where you and the other men were brought in that school area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I've concluded with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After you arrived and the people on your bus and the people in your convoy, did other Muslim men continue to arrive and continue to enter into the gymnasium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but when it dawned, after it had dawned, the groups were still being brought in and they were taken into the gymnasium as well. This lasted until I don't remember what time, but after that, at one point General Mladic appeared at the door, and because we were very crowded in that gymnasium and because we were not given any bread or water, we cried out, all in one voice, "Why are you torturing us here?" And then he said, "Well, your government does not want you, and I have to take care of you." One group of you will be taken to Kladusa, to Fikret Abdic, and one group will be transported to Bijeljina. You will also be given water when you get out of the gym. He left, and then later --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you right there for just a second. Can you estimate the number of men who were in the gym with you when the gym was at its fullest capacity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 2.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at any point in time while you were in that gymnasium, did Bosnian Serb soldiers come into the gymnasium and shoot their weapons, shoot their guns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. We would from time to time start shouting, because we couldn't take it anymore. We were suffocating. There was no air, there was no water. And then we would start shouting and they would then open fire and shoot above our heads. And then everything would be silent for a while and they would say, "Just keep quiet, else you will all be shot."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness N, continue describing what occurred to you and to the other men at that gymnasium, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the Bosnian Serbs who were standing guard issued some orders. There was a group of them standing to the left of the door, of the main door, and they ordered men to get out of the gymnasium through that door. They said that they would be taken somewhere. And the Bosnian Serb soldiers then brought some stripes of cloth with which they blindfolded us, and they gave some people some water and left somewhere. A column would march for a while and then it would stop, and this would last for a couple of minutes and then another column would be leaving the gymnasium after that. When people starting getting out, we heard somewhere, coming from the distance, bursts of gunfire. Then it would stop, then everything would be quiet for a while, and after a while we would hear rifles being fired again, again at the same spot. And some elderly people said at that point, "They're taking everyone. They're killing everyone." And in the evening hours, between 7.00, 7.30 p.m., it was my turn to leave the gymnasium, together with some other people. I drank some water, and I was blindfolded, and I boarded a small truck which is called tamic. After it got full, it set out, and a red vehicle was following the truck and there was one soldier with an automatic rifle there and he was threatening us. He didn't let us speak. He said, "I will kill you all." We did not travel for very long. At one point we turned off the road and went into a field, where we saw a lot of dead people. The TAM truck stopped and two Serb soldiers approached the truck. They opened the backside of the truck and they ordered us to get out. And I was the last one in the truck, so I was taken out first. And they showed me where I was supposed to stand, next to some dead bodies. And everybody was lined up like that, in several rows, with their backs facing them. The tamic left immediately, and immediately after it had left, we heard automatic rifles being fired. Everybody fell down at that point, and those who were not killed, who were still giving some signs of life, were shot at individually, were killed individually. I didn't dare move. I was just looking downwards towards the ground. And when the TAM truck left, when it moved, I turned around and I realised that it was taking people to another location. It was the same kind of truck, the same TAM truck, and it was also followed by a red car. And after a while the red car came back, and a little later this same TAM truck came to my location and it brought people to our location again, some 10 to 15 meters away from me. Men were again being ordered out of the truck and taken out. And the red car also stopped and Ratko Mladic got out of the car, together with the soldiers who were accompanying him, and they were watching people being taken out of the TAM truck and being lined up and executed. After they had finished their job, Ratko Mladic sat down in the same red car and he went back in the direction of the gymnasium. They continued bringing people and killing people and this lasted until dusk. Behind my back there was an excavator who was digging a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me interrupt you right there for a minute, Witness N. I want to clarify a couple of points in your testimony. You said when you left the school, a blindfold was put over your eyes, and you testified when you were in the truck in route to the execution field, you could see a red car that was following you. How was it, if you were blindfolded, you could see a red car that was following you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was blindfolded, immediately when they had blindfolded me, I moved the blindfold a little bit upwards so that I could see. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). But they weren't paying much attention to whether people were taking off their blindfolds or not. They were simply telling us not to talk and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness N, can you describe the soldiers who were the executioners? How were they dressed; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. They were dressed in dark green camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let's carry on with your account of the events on the 14th of July. You said, before I interrupted you, that you had seen some kind of mechanical equipment doing something. Could you tell the Judges what you saw and what you saw it doing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw an excavator. It was behind my back. It had a bucket, a kind of shovel. And it's a kind of machine that can both dig into the earth and also transport various material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you saw that excavator, was it dark outside or was it light?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And how long did that excavator work in your vicinity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: It worked until nightfall. When it became dark, another excavator arrived and they switched on their headlights. At that point, they were bringing bodies to one location only, and they were killing people at that location and the lights of the excavators were on and they kept killing men. And this continued until they finished off everyone. And when the last TAM truck arrived, somebody said, "That's it, there's no one left." One of the Serb soldiers asked, "Are we going back with you?" And this other man replied, "No, you're not going back with me. Maybe there will be another truck coming back to pick you up, and then you will go back. If it doesn't show up, then you will have to stand guard all night." Then after the truck had left, they remained standing and smoking next to the excavator. After that, a similar truck arrived with its lights on and I could hear people talk, but I didn't make out what they were saying. Then they switched off their lights, and we could see well, because it was moonlight. Then everybody sat down in the excavator and the truck and they went in the direction of the gymnasium. After they had left, I stood up and I started shouting. I wanted to see if there was anyone alive so we could leave together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before we get to that part of your testimony, do I understand your testimony correctly, then, that while the excavators were working and while it was dark, additional men, Muslim men were being brought to the execution site and were being executed in the front of the lights of these excavators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me show you two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And before I show you these exhibits, Mr. Dubuisson, it will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 20/5 and 20/8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Immediately behind the execution field where the men had been killed, can you describe the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Not yet, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the terrain, Witness N. Was it level, was it -- did it have other types of physical features?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more or less level, flat; not completely, but almost. But where the excavator was digging, there was a slope, a little hill. There wasn't much grass on it. It was a kind of field and it was not completely flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And behind the grass field, what was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a small forest above the area where the excavator was working, up the hill, up the slope, a small forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were at the execution site, did you notice any unique kind of physical structure that was in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed a kind of iron fence, iron railing. I don't know whether it was part of a bridge or whether it was just a fence that was there as a kind of protection. This is what I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I've shown you Prosecutor's Exhibit 20/5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if you could put that on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to see this; is that correct, Witness N?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I saw the same fence there in the immediate vicinity of the grave where the execution site was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now could you next place Prosecutor's Exhibit 20/8 on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see that same fence in Prosecutor's Exhibit 20/8?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you point it out, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, the small rail above the tunnel leading underneath the railroad tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness N. Now, therefore, does this location that's depicted in this photograph appear to you to be the same location where you were at the time of the executions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's the same location where the executions took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness N, I interrupted you when you had testified that you had stood up after everybody had left. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called out is there anyone alive for us to go? And one nearby answered back and said he was alive. He got up, and we left that location and crossed the pastures and turned left uphill into a wood there. In the wood, we sat down to have a rest. And then we heard shots at the same spot. The man with me said, "There they are. They've come back again." And I said "Let them." Then we saw another shot closer to us. And then he said, "They must have seen our traces through the high grass," because there was moonlight. As we felt them coming after us, we turned to the right and entered a thick thicket on our stomachs. They were following us, they shot into the woods, and then we wondered where we should go. And then we thought let's go to the railway track and retrace our steps. The railway track was immediately nearby. So when they went back to the place where they started shooting, we got up and went through the woods towards Tuzla. So the next day, when it dawned, another man appeared on the hill who had been there at the execution site like us. He joined us and continued with us and we crossed into free territory at Nezvuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date was the 19th. I think it was a Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, one last question: When you stood up, were you able to look around the execution field and were you able to estimate the number of bodies that were laying in that field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed to us that there were more than we had seen in the gym. That's what it looked like to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Witness N, I've concluded my examination of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now it's the time for the Defence lawyers to examine you, Witness N. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Witness N, you are now going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Petrusic, the Defence counsel for Mr. Krstic. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and good morning Your Honours; my learned friends from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you reached the warehouse in Bratunac on the 12th of July, people started to be taken out in the evening, Muslims started to be taken out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: They took out Hamdija Efendic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Hamed Efendic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Hamed. Hamed Efendic was the president of the Party of Democratic Action of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did they look for him by name and take him out because he was the president?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought him there separately, and they called him out specifically to come out, but they didn't say why he was being taken out, whether it was because he was the president or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was it your conclusion that that was the reason why they took him out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Hamed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: A rifle shot was heard and one of those, your Serb soldiers said, "He's killed, he's finished. Don't shoot again."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the others that were taken out were called out by their first and last names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Or were they called out by the village they came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So they were looking for particular people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from particular places.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: They looked for Ibran Mustafic as well, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Ibran Mustafic was politically very active, I think. He was president of the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In one of your earlier statements, you said that they killed Ibran Mustafic and that he didn't come back --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he didn't come back. What happened to him, there was a kind of argument heard between him and the Serb guards. He didn't come back into the gym. What happened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You also said that you heard from soldiers who were outside, the words "he's finished"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness N, I should like to show you the statement you gave to the State Security Service in Tuzla on the 25th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be Exhibit D-17.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Your Honours, it is page two which has been highlighted, the second sentence in the highlighted passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness N, this is your statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The second sentence in the highlighted part in the first paragraph says, "After that, they called out Ibran Mustafic, son of Mujo, former head of Srebrenica municipality and deputy in the BH parliament, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and killed him with a blunt object. I did not see them beat him, but I heard the blows and his cries and a Chetnik who said, 'He's finished.'" Did you make that statement to the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly I can't remember, but I'm not denying that I said that as well, because if that is what I said, that is what they said; I didn't add or detract from anything that I personally did not see or hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But Ibran Mustafic is alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness N, during those days, you saw General Mladic on a number of occasions, you even spoke to him; I could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only once I asked him a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: One of those questions was on the 13th of July, 1995, in the warehouse, after you had spent the night in the warehouse in Bratunac, in the morning, when you addressed him with the words: "What are you doing with us? Why are you killing people? Why are you not taking us to be exchanged?" This is also from the same statement that you made, the second paragraph of the English version. MR. PETRUSIC [Interpretation] And both Your Honours and the Prosecutor have this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What was General Mladic's reply to your statement that people were being killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "You will no longer be killed. It was not possible to come to an agreement earlier on. If that agreement had been reached, this wouldn't have happened. We have come to an agreement now. You're going to Kalisija. Count yourselves so that I can designate transportation."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did he ask you who was killing men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your further contacts, did you tell him that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When they -- I may be wrong, but I think it was on the 14th of July when they brought you to this meadow for execution. You again saw Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to place on the ELMO Prosecutor's Exhibit 20/8, for the witness to try to explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, on this photograph, where did that tamic come to a halt, the small truck that brought you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly here, somewhere here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the witness is pointing to the far right side of the photograph, midway up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Where did they take your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That is where the truck stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And where did they take your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: My group, here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: How far was that from the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which truck, because the truck didn't come once; as the truck moved away, the next groups came, because they were killing one after another. If the first truck was five to ten meters, about five meters, then the second came, and the third was up here [indicates]. And they went on like that, in a line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So in relation to the truck, and you told us the spot where it was, your group was executed right next to the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the truck moved away, the group was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please, where was your body, or rather in what position was it in relation to this small thicket we see to the left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: My head was turned this way and my legs towards the thicket.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is clear for the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And so from that position you saw Mladic arriving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you able to hear him say anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not, because the truck's engine was still on while they were unloading the men, so that the engine was on and I couldn't hear whether he was talking or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You remained on that spot for several hours, until the last group that arrived was executed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what somebody said: When the last truck arrived, there were no more, that it was all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you didn't move from there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. When night fell and when they turned on the lights, I took shelter. It was cloudy and it started to drizzle, so the lights were not on me, and I drew myself from under that dead pile and I went to the left. And after a couple of meters I was free and I lay there until they finished it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you abandoned the spot; you left the spot where you were originally and moved a couple of meters away. From that spot did you notice anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed a truck coming, with men, and saw the dead in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you see from that spot Ratko Mladic coming four or five times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your statement that you have before you that you saw four or five times -- just a moment, please. Just a moment, please. We're talking about a particular time and place, this particular place, where you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think in the English version that is page 3, and the last highlighted paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: -- and I quote: "While I lay there, the blood of the dead was covering me. The Chetniks were bringing new groups in the tamic and killing them. "When dark fell, about an hour after I had been brought there, I took advantage of the Chetniks' carelessness and crawled into some bushes, where I hid. From that place I saw them bringing new groups in a tamic and killing them by the light of the headlights of the two excavators, as they had also brought a second excavator to this spot. While I lay there, I saw Ratko Mladic, bareheaded, come up behind the tamic four or five times in a red car and watch the executions."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation is wrong. A red car escorted every tamic, and Ratko Mladic appeared only once. And I saw Ratko Mladic in all six times, so this must be an error in the translation. I never said that Ratko Mladic came every time. And there was a red car escorting each of the tamic trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness N, I wasn't showing you the translation; I was showing you your statement given to the State Security Service of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no more questions. Witness N, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Harmon, any additional questions, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just a few, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, you were asked by my colleague about the individual named Hamed Efendic, who was the president of the SDA political party in Srebrenica. Was Mr. Efendic an influential member of the Srebrenica Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the war, he was. When the war started, he had no authority; other people were in command of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand, but was he an esteemed and highly regarded member of the community even though he didn't have a political position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. If he did have a political position, he didn't have any political influence. He wasn't particularly held in high esteem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ibran Mustafic, who was the former head of the Srebrenica municipality and was a deputy in the Bosnia-Herzegovina parliament, was he someone who was influential and esteemed within the Muslim community of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was until the war. He was more esteemed. But when the war started, he meant nothing for Srebrenica either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after the -- strike that. While you were in the warehouse, you said that the Bosnian Serbs would come in and they would call out the names of individuals. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you know all of the individuals whose names were being called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know any one of them, any one of those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that, at least in part, when the Bosnian Serbs were calling out names, that they were selecting people who they were fully aware of and who they wanted to identify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called out the name of the village and they would say, "People from that village should get up." Whether those people who got up knew one another, I don't know. But before that, they would come and they would know one another, but I didn't know our men, nor the Serb soldiers. I didn't know either. They spoke to each other as if they were acquaintances: "Where are you? Where have you been? Where's your family?" And then this man on our side would ask the soldier about his family, and that is how they spoke. But I didn't know anyone among the Serb soldiers or among the people -- the Bosniaks who were talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness N, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, I have a couple of questions, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness N.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to understand perhaps globally the main features of your testimony; first, the phases of execution you mentioned. I'm trying to follow you. You said they would be calling on some important people, prominent people, they would go out, you would hear cries, they would not come back. And you mentioned Hamed Efendic and Ibran Mustafic, or whatever. These people, if I understood rightly, were privileged to have special treatment, to be tortured or anything, but they were selected. The second phase were people coming out in lines, blindfolded, and you were not among them yet. These people, if I understood rightly, were called upon from villages, asking each group to come, but not by names. And if I understood rightly, they were executed immediately out, because you heard the fire while you were inside and they never came back. Then at 7.30 you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- were blindfolded and you went in a small truck. I understand this was a third phase, people taken away to be executed. And the truck would go back and bring other people, you mentioned. They would be put on rows and so on. Did I understand you rightly? Was that exactly the evolution of the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the people were getting out of the gym, they were being blindfolded. First they would give the person some water, and then afterwards he would be blindfolded and then we would get on a truck. And this continued for a while until they finished. And we were then taken, still blindfolded, to a field, a pasture, where we were then being lined up and executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The bottom line is that everybody in the gym finished by going out, because you stated 7.30.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Everybody, because you also mentioned that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people remained in the gym after me, and people were still being brought in after me. And at one point somebody said, "It's all over," when the last truck full of people came. And then the man asked the soldier whether he wanted to go back with him, and he said he wouldn't, and he said that maybe there would be another truck coming back and that they would go back; if not, they would stay there and keep guard all night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I understood. I just want to know the selection which happened at the beginning, which included prominent people, was just at the beginning, taking them out, and then you hear them suffering and shouting. But after that there was no selection; everybody was taken out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that everybody was taken out. There were people who wanted to go first because they were so thirsty. They just wanted to get some water. They didn't care whether they would be killed or not. But they didn't let us do that. There was supposed to be a line; only once you have reached the entrance you could get some water. There was a small room there with a table in it where people were being given water, and at the same time two soldiers would be blindfolding the person. And after that the person was taken to the TAM truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I understood that. So they were all taken. But then you mentioned that when you looked at the field after the executions took place, you found more dead people than there were in the gym, so not only all the people in the gym were killed, but apparently other people came from other places. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is how it seemed because we were crowded in the gym while we were in the gym, and the group appeared to be larger once we were in the field, but it wasn't. They were not bringing people from elsewhere. But because people were so crammed in the gymnasium, it didn't seem that they were -- that there were that many. But once they were lying dead on the field, the number seemed greater. This is only how it seemed but they were not bringing other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But it was all the people in the gym in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the people from the gym, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that in the gym there were some people that could hardly move. You said they were over 60, but people over 60 can move. Were they also executed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those who got out of the gym were killed, whether they were young or old. As soon as they could get up and reach the truck, they were taken away. And afterwards, they didn't have to walk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you saw them being taken away, you saw them being taken away. They were not spared; children or old people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no children, and the elderly people were not spared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you heard the soldiers at a certain stage introducing themselves to one another. Do you remember what they said, which divisions they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because I heard you saying that some of them were saying they belonged to the wolves and others say, "We belong to Arkanovac."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes, I did say that. That is how they addressed each other. We didn't call them that way. It was the way they were addressing each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What did they say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would say, for example, "This one is an Arkanovac," and then the man would say, "Yes, I am." And he would ask him then, "Are you from the Drina Wolves or some other wolves," I don't know, and then he said, "Yes, I am, and I'm not ashamed of it." This is how they were addressing each other, but I didn't know where they were from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you remember some of the names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But why did you mention Drina Wolves then? Did they mention it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Among themselves. Did you notice any accent? Were these an accent of Bosnia or Croatia or Serbia or you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. All those accents were the same for me. I am not very familiar with different accents. I don't know where people come from. All I can tell is that they are from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think you served before in the Bosnian army, you said, so you don't know the accents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were in the Bosnian army or in the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I served in the Yugoslav army, and during the war before the area became protected, I served with the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, just for our knowledge, how long -- you said that you stayed without moving until all the soldiers went away. How long did this last, staying without moving, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't tell you exactly how long, but it was quite dark, so it must have been around 11.00 p.m. but I cannot be precise. And after that, I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness N, I would just like to clear one point in your answer to Judge Riad. I thought I heard you testify that when the soldiers were saying, "I am from the Arkan," or "I am Drina Wolves," that was in the Bratunac warehouse not in the gym at Zvornik; is that right? That's -- when I read over my notes of your testimony yesterday --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- yes, I just wanted to clear that up, where that happened, okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The second question I have is: You said that the soldiers at the execution site wore dark green camouflage uniforms. And before that, you said that the soldiers around the gym guarding you or transporting you wore green camouflage uniforms. Was there a difference between those two kinds of uniforms of those that were performing the executions and those that were transporting or guarding you or were they the same kind of green camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one man in the red vehicle which was following the TAM truck who was wearing a one colour grey uniform. Everybody else wore multicoloured camouflage uniforms and this other man was wearing a grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. But the ones that wore the green camouflage uniforms, it was the same kind of uniforms; the men doing the executing and the men guarding and transporting. Okay. Now, when General Mladic came to the gym and said that the prisoners would be transported -- would be exchanged, how much time lapsed between then and the time that they brought in the blindfolds and began to take the men out blindfolded to the execution field? It was the same day, you testified, but how much time would you say between the time Mladic came and said you were going to go to a prisoner exchange in the gym, and then when they brought in the blindfolds and began to get people ready to go to the execution field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were in the warehouse in Bratunac, he told us that we would be exchanged and that we should count ourselves, and that transport would be provided. But this is not where they brought the blindfolds, not in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that. But you also testified, you also testified both today, and in your earlier statement that when you were in the gym, when you were in the gym in Zvornik, that Mladic came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So I'm asking you what was the time between that time when he came in the gym and talked about -- you said he talked about saying that you would be exchanged and the time they began to blindfold you and take you in the trucks to the execution field. Was it an hour, two hours, or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the gym, Mladic did not say that we would be exchanged. He said that we would be sent to Kladusa and Bijeljina and it was only in Bratunac that he said that we would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. But the question remains: How much time between whatever he said in the gym and the time when they began to take you out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And my last question to you is: At the execution site, you said that Mladic did come in a red car. How long did he stay in your -- how long did you observe him to say at the execution site? You testified today one time you saw him in the red car at the execution site.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stayed until all men were taken off the TAM truck and until they were all executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, roughly how much time did that take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were 25 to 30 people that had to be taken off the TAM truck, and then they had to line them up and execute them. I don't know how much time that would be. You could perhaps judge for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I was not there; you were. The -- would you say half an hour, an hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Pardon the interruption, Mr. President, but I was examining the transcript as Judge Wald was asking questions, and there was no answer recorded on the transcript to Judge Wald's question about whether the people who were wearing the green camouflage uniforms at the execution sites were wearing the same kind of green camouflage uniforms guarding and transporting the prisoners. To that question put by Judge Wald to Witness N, there was no answer recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Would you answer that question now then so we can have a complete record, whether or not the uniforms of the men performing the execution of the soldiers at the execution field were the same as those that were guarding you at the gym, same army camouflage uniforms. You're nodding your head; is that yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Judge Wald, and thank you, Mr. Harmon, for your intervention. Witness N, I also have a few questions for you. My first question is the following: You arrive at the school, people get off the bus and you told us that at that point, they were mostly men. Why do you say "mostly"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there were no children or women with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were only men. My second question is a synthetical one. How many times did you see Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Six times. Could you then tell us where it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I saw him was when I was separated and taken to an unfinished house. The second time was when we were being put on the buses in Potocari, he was standing next to the buses. The third time it was when he came to us and he told us that we would be exchanged in Kalesija. The fourth time was when we were boarding the buses; again, he was standing right next to the buses. The fifth time was when he came to the gym and when he told us that some of us would go to Kladusa and some of us would go to Bijeljina. And the sixth time was at the meadow where we were executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. You can still see Prosecutor's Exhibit 20/8 on the monitor. Mr. Usher, maybe the monitor of the witness could be switched on. Witness, could you please have a look at the photograph. The one that is on the screen. And to tell us the following: We know exactly where you were but what I would like to know is where exactly was General Mladic when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was here at this location [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say that he was right next to these yellow marks somewhere midway up the photograph. You have already told us that that is exactly the spot where you were as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were there at the point that you're indicating and where was Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was lying like this. My head was here [indicates] my legs facing the forest, and Mladic was standing to my right. And the people who were unloading the TAM truck were here [indicates], and he was standing right next to the TAM truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Could you then tell us how far from you was General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than ten metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. Thank you very much. My next question for you is the following: I think I have understood you correctly, but I would like, nevertheless, to have a confirmation. When General Mladic arrived here at this location, he was able to see the results of the execution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then when he arrived, you told us that the buses were coming from the right side on the photograph and that a line was being formed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the truck?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the truck. And then after the people, the truck had left, people would be lined up and executed. So when General Mladic arrived here, could you tell us how many rows of people were there already?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't count, Your Honour. I didn't count. All I know is that there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could you perhaps give us an estimate? Do you have an idea as to the number of journeys that the truck made; how many times the truck arrived to this spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I had been brought to the spot, you mean? No, no, I cannot give you a definite answer. I was in great fear. I wasn't counting people. I couldn't think about that. All I know is that it was on several occasions, maybe even as many as ten times that they brought people in, but I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. But maybe you will be able to answer the following question: When you arrived at the execution site, had there already been corpses there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much, Witness N. I don't have any other questions for you. You have been asked a number of questions by both parties and by the Judges, and you have answered all of those questions. Is there anything else that you would like to say? Anything that has not been brought up, something you haven't had the opportunity to say? If you wish to say something, you can do it now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have anything else to say. I have said everything I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness N, thank you very much. There is a technical matter that we have to attend to and after that you will be free to go. Mr. Petrusic, I believe that we have one Defence exhibit, D-17.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence would like to tender D-17 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Subject to a number of redactions which identify this witness by name and by other features, we would have no objection. I have gone through this in the examination. I can give a copy to the registrar of the redactions that are necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit D-17 there will therefore be admitted into evidence under seal and there will also be a redacted version which will be made available to the public. Mr. Dubuisson, will you take care of that? Very well, thank you. Witness N, you have completed your testimony here before the International Tribunal. Thank you very much for coming to testify, and we are so glad you survived the execution and we hope that you will have a happy life after this. At least in order to -- to be able to tell the world that the things that happened independently of those who had committed them are condemnable, are horrible, must not happen again. Thank you very much, once again. Please do not move. Let us see what's happening with our next witness, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have another witness. He will be a protected witness, and if we could take perhaps ten additional minutes during the break for reasons that are required, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of protective measures will be applied, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Harmon, you asked for an additional ten minutes. I was actually going to have a break. The break was supposed to be 15 minutes. Do you need any additional time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We need an additional ten minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty-five minutes. So just for the public, there will be a 25-minute break now and after that we will resume with the same protective measures for our next witness. Twenty-five minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to hand to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Witness. The registrar is going to show you your name, written on a piece of paper. You're going to read that name and say only yes or no whether that is your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you being treated well here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we shall continue to do so. Now, Witness O, you are going to answer questions which Mr. Cayley is going to put to you. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I know you're feeling very nervous at the moment. Relax as best you can. Let me let you into a little secret. Whenever I stand up in this courtroom, I feel exactly the same way; the only difference is that I've learned to hide it over the years. This may be the only opportunity that you get to tell this account. Don't worry if you can't remember things. I'll remind you. Just relax, speak slowly, and tell the Judges what happened to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: I will. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you're Bosnian by nationality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you're Muslim by faith; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think in 1992 the Serbs overran the town of Nova Kasaba and you and your family had to move; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's where you were living with your family in 1992, in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you and your family lived in a number of places, and then in July of 1995 you found yourself in the village of Slapovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you were going to school in the town of Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes, that is right; I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In July of 1995 I think you had just turned your 17th birthday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes, on the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I want you to think back to July of 1995, and specifically to the 11th of July, the 11th of that month. Do you recall that on that day the Bosnian Serb army overran the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think on that day you and your father decided to go to the woods with the other able-bodied men from Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes. We decided like many others. I don't know whether I was able-bodied, but I decided to go there, because if I had gone to the UN Compound, I don't know whether I would have been saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the reason that you went to the woods is because you feared for your life; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in the village of Jaglici, where the column formed to go through the woods, can you tell the Judges about the degree of organisation of that column, as you remember it now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: The degree of organisation was almost nonexistent. The BH army -- I don't know whether I can call it an army, because many were unarmed -- they were preparing for a breakthrough to form a column and then civilians followed them. But it was chaotic, so that it was only in the morning of the 12th of July, or rather at 11.00, that I left Jaglici in the group of the last one or two thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was your father in the Bosnian army at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member, but he didn't have a uniform, he didn't have a rifle. I don't know whether I could call him a soldier. He was just formerly a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I know you've told me that the column moved through the forests on the 12th of July of 1995, and I'm not going to ask you questions about that, although the Defence and the Judges may have some questions for you. I want you to think about the 13th of July of 1995, in the afternoon, when you and some others gave yourselves up to the Bosnian Serb soldiers on the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. Can you tell the Judges how you gave yourselves up to the Bosnian Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, after heavy shelling throughout the night, many people were killed. There was general confusion. We didn't know where to go. There was a big forest, and about 10.00 a loudspeaker was heard. Probably, I assume, they were Bosnian Serb soldiers, saying that we should surrender, otherwise we would all be killed and the shelling would continue, and that we would be treated in accordance with all the Geneva Conventions, they said. We stayed in the woods until 3.00. They repeated the message I don't know how many times over the loudspeaker, but around 3.00 a sort of column was formed which went down. They weren't people with weapons. Some people may have had weapons, but as far as I could see, there was general chaos. There were many who were wounded, perhaps more than those who were not. And we came out at the village of Kamenica, where we could hear tanks and APCs moving around the road. But I didn't see them until we got closer. This was a long column. I didn't see people surrendering. I couldn't see the end of the column. We were carrying the wounded. And I didn't yet know that we were surrendering. I knew we were going somewhere; I didn't know where. When we got closer, I saw that there were tanks and some other weapons on wheels. I don't know what kind. The column was continuous, and then I realised that we had surrendered. When I got close to the bridge, there were five or six, or maybe four or seven -- I don't know -- soldiers, roughly, there, and they said -- the column was moving and they were talking, and they were saying, "Come on." I had a bag. One of the soldiers asked me, "What do you have in your bag? Do you have any weapons or German marks or something?" I said I didn't. They told us to put our bags aside, our weapons, to lay down our weapons and any sharp objects. But I didn't see anyone with weapons. I think no one had weapons. And they told us that everything would be returned to us. Rows were formed on one side of the road, along the stream, close to the bridge. There were five rows of roughly 100 meters each. I can't tell you exactly. It might have been 90, 100, 110. The wounded were there too, and there may have been more of them than us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony that there were five or six soldiers who were around and about the Muslim men who had come to the road. Do you recall now how those soldiers were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: They had uniforms on, camouflage uniforms. I don't know whether they had -- all wore one-piece uniforms, but they were camouflage. That's as much as I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it blue camouflage or green/brown camouflage? Do you recall now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: It was more olive-green or brown. It wasn't blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after these columns were formed on the road when you gave to the Judges an estimate of the size, what happened to you all next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: When all the men had come out -- and there was no interruption. There was a column constantly coming out. And while they were coming out, the Bosnian Serb soldiers were, in quotation marks, "good, decent." They didn't curse anyone, they didn't mistreat anyone. Because otherwise someone might have escaped. While I was standing in a line, we had to raise our arms as soon as we left our bags. Very close to me there was a tank, and one or two weapons on wheels with some sort of machine-guns or something; I don't know exactly. And on the tank, in white letters, the words "queen of death" was written. I think it was in Cyrillic, but I can't be a hundred per cent sure. And next to the river -- again I can't tell you the exact number of soldiers; ten, maybe fewer, who had their guns pointed at us. There were soldiers walking past us, asking for money, and when everyone handed everything over, they cursed our balija mothers, "Balija son, we'll show you," and things like that. Almost everyone, each one of them, made these demands. I remember one in particular who had a machine-gun and an ammunition belt which was almost down to the ground. And then two passenger cars appeared. I think they were a Golf, Golfs. One was a police car and one was a metallic grey. Soldiers were sitting on the roofs and inside. There were a number of them -- I don't know -- five, six, or ten. They got out. Some of them had camouflage but police uniforms, so they were camouflage blue. And others were like the others, in army uniforms, that is, olive-green or brownish camouflage. Some of them may have also asked for things. I didn't see them beat anyone. They may have, they may have not. In the meantime, I saw buses which had come up to those lines in the direction of the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje, but they probably couldn't pass because of us. I don't know the exact number of buses there were and trucks, because there was a curve in the road, so we couldn't see them all. And then we were ordered to run along the road towards Bratunac. We didn't know where we were going at the time. And so we ran and we carried the wounded as we ran. We took turns, with our hands up. And when I reached the bus, I saw that there were women and children inside from Potocari, from the UN Compound. I recognised them by their clothing and I recognised a schoolmate of mine in the bus, in the window. So as we ran, we had to lift three fingers, and the soldiers were running alongside, with rifles. And I think the drivers in the bus and the trucks were armed with weapons, but I'm not sure of that. I can't say for sure. I thought they were. So we had to show the sign of three fingers so that -- as we passed the trucks, so that the women and children would see us. And so we ran for about one kilometer. We passed those buses and trucks. As I said, I don't know how many there were. Maybe ten, maybe fewer. I don't know. And we reached a spot where we turned left. Behind me a Bosnian Serb soldier asked the man behind me -- I couldn't see who he was. I don't know what he looks like. Whether he was young or old, I don't know. He asked him, "Which unit were you in in Srebrenica?" He was probably referring to the army. The man said, "I was in an infantry unit." I don't know why he said that. It sounds ironic. An execution unit, actually. Then the blows started. I don't know whether he stayed there or continued running. I don't know. As we turned to the left, I saw a dead man. He wasn't run over, because the cars were only using one lane, but he must have been killed much earlier, because there were flies all over him and worms. He seemed to me to be like an older man, but I can't say for sure. Then we turned left, running all the time. We were carrying the wounded, I, among others. We took turns. I don't know whether we, all of us, left the place where we had stood, where we had surrendered. And the place where we turned was on a meadow above the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. The grass was quite high, but it had been stamped on as if people had been there before. I just remember that, that it wasn't standing up, the grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could wait there one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 1/E/1 which is a small map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you saw a number of buses travelling on the road full of women and children. In which direction were those buses travelling; can you recall now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes. They were going along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje. That was the direction. Bratunac to Konjevic Polje direction, I think that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, you said that the Bosnian Serb soldiers made you essentially put your fingers up in a -- three fingers you had to raise above your head. Do you know what the significance of that three-fingered salute was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: I don't really know how to explain. It's a sign of theirs. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you can look at the map next to you, and if you could first of all indicate to the Judges -- in fact if the map could be moved up, please. If you could indicate approximately where you came down, where you surrendered to the Serbs. That's the first point I'd like you to indicate, just approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Somewhere here [indicates] near Sandici. And then we ran up to Sandici. I don't know whether we actually reached Sandici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could wait there, Witness. I just need to read into the record the point that you're making on the map. If you could indicate again where you came down from the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness is indicating on this exhibit a point approximately halfway between Sandici and where the road intersects with the Nova Kasaba-Konjevic Polje road and that is on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: No, no, not really halfway. It was up to a point maybe one kilometre away from Sandici, so not quite halfway.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me and making the record more accurate. Can you indicate to the Judges where the meadow was as best you can recollect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: I can't show you on the map. It was in Sandici somewhere. There are five or ten houses there, it's not a proper settlement. I just know there were about two or three or maybe five, six houses around me, I can't tell you exactly. There was a house on the lower side of the road. I saw that later while I was sat -- while I sat there. While we were running I didn't see it, I saw it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So if you were facing Bratunac, the meadow was on the left-hand side of the road and it was very close to the settlement of Sandici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the left-hand side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said that when you arrived in the meadow, the grass was high but that you could see that the grass had been flattened. What did you think at the time when you saw that the grass had been flattened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: I thought that perhaps some other people had been there, maybe a group prior to ours. That is what occurred to me. It wasn't flattened as if trucks had passed there, but rather as if people had played ball there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you could remember while we are proceeding to try and speak slowly. I know you do naturally speak very quickly, but there are interpreters in between us, and it makes their task much easier if you and I both speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll slow down. Sometimes I sort of get excited, and then I speed up a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're being very clear. You're being very clear, but just if you could speak more slowly that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you went into this meadow. Can you remember how many of you there were in the meadow, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact number of people in the meadow, but where we were standing at the road, according to my assessment, there was between 1.000 and 2.000. It was -- I'm sure it was more than 1.000, but I can't tell you the exact number but there certainly were very many. We were right next to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after you all gathered in the meadow, what happened to you next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Soldiers surrounded us, soldiers of the Bosnian Serbs. Actually, people first sat down. I was somewhere in the middle further to the back, actually. And here again, there were a large number of people, but I can't tell you how many. And I don't know whether all of us had come in one group from the place where we were before, where we -- when we ran. There was a tank in front of us again. I saw it when I was sitting. I don't remember whether it was there when we ran up. In front were the wounded. And one of the Bosnian Serb soldiers started saying something. I didn't register everything because I wasn't interested. But something to the effect, "We are from Serbia." Actually, he first asked whether there was anyone who needed bandaging and he bandaged our wounded; or rather, I'm sorry, whether there was anyone who could bandage the wounded. And then a man offered to do that. Then he searched him with a pistol in his hand. He searched the man. This soldier had a black bandanna on his head or a scarf tied at the nape of his neck. He was a very heavily-built man, well-built man. I think he wore a camouflage uniform as well. I'm not sure whether it was in one piece or trousers separate, I can't tell. I think he was fair. I came to that conclusion on the basis of his beard. He didn't have a beard but he had a growth of hair as if he hadn't shaven. And later he said, "You see what happened to your comrades. If you had surrendered, you wouldn't have had so many wounded." I can't quote him exactly, but I'm paraphrasing. Later he said, "Other soldiers will come now. They won't hurt you." When he said that, he probably meant another unit. I don't know. I can't tell. But they were the same soldiers -- not the same, but they wore the same uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we're still on the 13th of July of 1995. Do you remember approximately what time the events that you're talking about now took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Which event do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm talking about now the Serb soldier addressing the crowd, the Serb soldier who asked the man if he could attend to the wounded. Do you remember what time of the day that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes, this was in the afternoon, perhaps 4.00, 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon. I don't know exactly. I didn't have a watch, and I don't know. Roughly that time of day it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Serb -- the Bosnian Serb soldier who asked if there was anybody who could attend to the wounded; do you recall that testimony? The man who assisted the wounded was a member of the Muslim men assembled on the meadow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: He was probably a Muslim, I don't know what he was, but he volunteered himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serb soldier who had the bandanna on his head explain to you all what was going to happen to all of you on the meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS O
utterances.text: Yes. He said that we would be transferred to a hangar or rather to hangars in Bratunac where we would spend the night. And the next day, we would be with our families, we would be exchanged and handed over, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
